title: Lesson 25: Responsible Use: Data Policy, Vendor Evaluation, and Accountability
description: The three pieces that keep AI defensible at organizational scale: a written data policy, a way to judge the vendors you standardize on, and a clear answer to who answers when something goes wrong.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Responsible Use: Data Policy, Vendor Evaluation, and Accountability", what are the three parts of responsible use at this scale?
options: A data policy that says what is allowed into the tool, vendor evaluation that says how you choose the tool, and accountability that says who answers when something goes wrong
Encryption, backups, and periodic access reviews
Training, licensing, and a support ticket queue
Prompt hygiene, output review, and server logging
questions.explanation: The lesson names those three pieces directly and frames them as the honest price of relying on the tool for work that involves clients, contracts, and other people's data.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say good individual habits stop being enough once a team standardizes on a tool?
options: Because individual habits are usually wrong

Because habits travel with one person while a policy has to travel with the team, and once a team leans on a tool for real work it becomes an organizational purchase whether or not anyone formally bought it
Because written policies are legally required in most jurisdictions
Because tools change too fast for habits to survive
questions.explanation: The lesson makes the conversion argument and then names the failure it prevents: a company depending on tools nobody evaluated and data nobody vetted, because people signed up with a work email on their own.

questions.question: What does the lesson identify as the fix when people have already adopted unvetted tools on their own?
options: Disciplining the people who did it
Banning AI tools until IT approves a single vendor
Giving them a better, approved path and making the rules clear, rather than scolding them
Leaving it alone, since individual use carries no organizational risk
questions.explanation: The lesson says pointedly that the fix is not to scold the people who found a useful tool, but to give them an approved path and clear rules.
